form.current-chamber: IN THE SENATE OF THE UNITED STATES

action.action-desc: Mr. Wyden (for himself, Mr. Whitehouse, Mr. Reed, and Mr. Coons) introduced the following bill; which was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources

form.official-title: To direct the Secretary of Energy to establish a program to advance energy storage deployment by reducing the cost of energy storage through research, development, and demonstration, and for other purposes.

section.text: This Act may be cited as the Reducing the Cost of Energy Storage Act of 2019.

subparagraph.text: The term DER means an electric device that can produce or consume energy that is located—

clause.text: on the distribution system or any subsystem of the distribution system; or
behind a customer meter.

subparagraph.text: The term DER includes—

clause.text: an energy storage resource;
an energy generation technology;
a demand response resource;
an energy efficiency resource;
an electric vehicle and associated supply equipment and systems; and
aggregations and integrated control systems, including virtual power plants, microgrids, and networks of microgrid cells.

paragraph.text: The terms electric consumer and State regulatory authority have the meanings given the terms in section 3 of the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 (16 U.S.C. 2602).
The term energy storage means equipment or facilities capable of absorbing energy, storing energy for a period of time, and dispatching the stored energy, that—

subparagraph.text: uses mechanical, electrochemical, hydroelectric, or thermal processes, as a single facility or as an aggregation of units, throughout the electric grid, including behind the meter to store energy generated at 1 time for use at a later time;

uses mechanical, electrochemical, hydroelectric, or thermal processes, as a single facility or as an aggregation of units, throughout the electric grid, including behind the meter to store energy generated from mechanical processes that would otherwise be wasted for delivery at a later time; or
stores thermal energy for direct use for heating or cooling at a later time in a manner that avoids the need to use electricity at that later time.

paragraph.text: The term light-duty consumer vehicle has the meaning given the term light-duty vehicle in section 1037.801 of title 40, Code of Federal Regulations (as in effect on the date of enactment of this Act).
The term microgrid means a localized grid that can disconnect from the traditional grid to operate autonomously and help mitigate grid disturbances to strengthen grid resilience.
The term program means the energy storage program established under section 3(a).
The term Secretary means the Secretary of Energy.
The term State energy office has the meaning given the term in section 124(a) of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 (42 U.S.C. 15821(a)).
The term transit vehicle has the meaning given the term bus in section 1192.3 of title 36, Code of Federal Regulations (as in effect on the date of enactment of this Act).

section.header: Reducing the cost of energy storage

paragraph.text: Not later than 1 year after the date of enactment of this Act, the Secretary shall establish a cross-cutting national program within the Department of Energy to advance energy storage deployment by reducing the cost of energy storage through research, development, and demonstration.

subsection.text: In developing the program, the Secretary shall consider the goals of—

subparagraph.text: reducing the full lifecycle cost and environmental impact of energy storage technologies, services, and applications, with an emphasis on reducing costs associated with combining energy storage with intermittent renewable energy generation; and
increasing the cost-competitiveness of energy storage technologies, services, and applications, including—

clause.text: the costs of subsystem components, installation, and integration; and
the costs associated with the application of energy storage technologies within integrated control systems;

paragraph.text: facilitating innovation in the manner in which energy storage systems are conceived, designed, manufactured, installed, and used for various energy services;
improving the understanding of the economics and technical characteristics of new electric grid operating principles enabled by energy storage, including by considering regional characteristics;

subparagraph.text: identifying the various use cases that are possible with energy storage (including individual technology applications, combination technology applications, and integrated control system applications); and
quantifying, demonstrating, and maximizing—

clause.text: the value of energy storage in the various use cases identified under subparagraph (A); and
the energy storage services that could be provided in those various use cases—

subclause.text: in multiple or stacked services, including the generation of multiple value streams from integrated control systems, such as microgrids;

paragraph.text: identifying, addressing, and reducing market barriers that limit energy storage adoption, including by—

subparagraph.text: identifying wholesale and retail market barriers;
helping to streamline processes—

clause.text: to reduce the time required for project completion; and
to lower interconnection costs; and

subparagraph.text: facilitating increased deployment of energy storage across sectors, including facilitating—

clause.text: the deployment of residential, commercial, and industrial applications; and
the deployment to low-income individuals and communities;

paragraph.text: advancing and validating the safety, reliability, and performance of energy storage, including by—

subparagraph.text: establishing procedures for evaluating, verifying, and reporting the performance of energy storage technologies, including the operational safety and usable life of energy storage technologies; and
refining existing or developing new industry-accepted codes, standards, and testing procedures to specify desired performance parameters for energy storage services;

paragraph.text: mapping pathways for energy storage deployment that increase the reliability, efficiency, security, and resilience of the electricity system, including by—

subparagraph.text: increasing the understanding of trends in electricity system inertia; and
assessing the ability of energy storage to provide the technical services needed for management of electricity system inertia;

paragraph.text: optimizing energy storage deployment—

subparagraph.text: to increase the deployment of variable renewable energy-generation technology and electric transportation; and
to support the optimal use of distributed and grid scale energy resources, including assessing the use of energy storage technologies to manage and optimize DERs—

clause.text: at different levels of market penetration; or
within integrated control systems or energy management systems, at different scales;

paragraph.text: advancing analytical resources to employ storage technology effectively and profitably, including by—

subparagraph.text: using existing integrated resource planning, transmission, and distribution design tools and other resources to build staff capacity for State regulatory authorities, State energy offices, electric utilities, balancing authorities, and Federal power marketing administrations to assist in reducing the uncertainty and risks relating to energy storage deployment;
developing techniques for conducting energy storage business case analyses; and
developing end-state modeling of least-cost solutions in scenarios in which—

clause.text: energy storage is deployed; and
90 to 100 percent of electricity is produced by renewable generation resources;

paragraph.text: spurring an increase in the number of energy storage technologies that are manufactured cost-competitively in the United States—

subparagraph.text: through public-private partnerships; and
by reducing investment risk;

paragraph.text: identifying—

subparagraph.text: critical and conflict materials issues relating to energy storage technologies; and
innovative, low-impact, and cost-competitive methods for procuring energy storage materials that address the conflict issues identified under subparagraph (A), including—

clause.text: materials recycling programs, which may also have the effect of increasing the life of batteries; and
novel methods for obtaining lithium and other minerals domestically; and

paragraph.text: enabling responsible lifecycle management of energy storage technologies through—

subparagraph.text: conducting research on responsible recycling of advanced battery materials and chemistries;
encouraging the sustainable design of new energy storage technologies; and
investigating end-of-life and second-life applications for advanced batteries.

subsection.text: In developing the program, the Secretary shall pay special attention to energy storage needs and opportunities that are relatively underdeveloped and potentially transformative for the electric grid.
The program shall be comprised of not fewer than 4 subprograms, including—

paragraph.text: a large-scale energy storage subprogram with emphasis on large-scale energy storage systems, including—

subparagraph.text: electrochemical storage;
pumped hydroelectric storage;
mechanical storage;
thermal storage;
compression storage; and
other technologies, as determined by the Secretary;

paragraph.text: a distributed storage subprogram that focuses on distributed energy storage technologies and applications, including existing assets and infrastructure, such as electric hot water heaters and thermal storage for space heating and cooling;
a transportation electrification subprogram that focuses on storage for and within electric vehicles, including—

subparagraph.text: light-, medium-, and heavy-duty passenger, utility, transit, and fleet vehicles;
vehicle-grid integration, including vehicle-to-grid applications and time-varying pricing signals; and
charging infrastructure and related networks and systems; and

paragraph.text: a responsible battery lifecycle management subprogram that focuses on—

subparagraph.text: recycling spent batteries, including all chemistries of batteries; and
designing new batteries for end-of-life recycling.

paragraph.text: The Secretary shall develop cost targets (including technology costs, installation costs, balance of services costs, and soft costs) for energy storage across all types of energy storage technology.
Not later than 5 years after the date of enactment of this Act and every 5 years thereafter, the Secretary shall—

subparagraph.text: increase the rigor of cost targets based on—

clause.text: a technology-neutral approach that considers all types of—

subclause.text: application and sector-specific use profiles; and
energy storage deployment scenarios, including individual technologies, technology combination use profiles, and integrated control system applications;

clause.text: input from a variety of stakeholders, including the stakeholders described in subsection (i);
the inclusion and use of existing infrastructure; and
the ability to optimize the integration of intermittent renewable energy generation technology and DERs; and

subparagraph.text: establish cost subtargets specific to technologies and applications selected by the Secretary, taking into consideration electricity market prices and what is required to be cost-competitive in specific markets for electric grid products and services.

paragraph.text: During the period beginning on the date of enactment of this Act and ending on the date on which the Secretary first increases the rigor of cost targets under paragraph (2), the default cost targets to be achieved by the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act, shall be an 80-percent reduction in the per kilowatt hour all-in installed cost of each energy storage technology class, as determined under paragraph (4).

subparagraph.text: Not later than 1 year after the date of enactment of this Act, the Secretary shall, based on input from the stakeholders described in subsection (i), establish categories of energy storage technologies for the purposes of—

clause.text: updating the cost targets under paragraph (2); and
assigning the default cost target under paragraph (3).

subparagraph.text: At a minimum, the Secretary shall establish the following energy storage technology classes under subparagraph (A):

clause.text: Electrochemical storage.
Pumped hydroelectric storage.
Mechanical storage.
Thermal storage.
Compression storage.

paragraph.text: Not later than 1 year after the date of enactment of this Act, the Secretary shall submit to Congress a report that includes a scoping plan for the organization of the program.
In preparing the report under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall confer with, and seek advice from, public and private stakeholders, such as the stakeholders described in subsection (i).

subsection.text: The Secretary shall submit to Congress an annual report that describes the progress of the program, including—

paragraph.text: a detailed summary of—

subparagraph.text: actions taken to address each goal listed in subsection (b); and
the outcomes of those actions;

paragraph.text: the quantity of energy storage deployed;
the administrative costs of the program;
the total amount of program funds awarded, including a description, by State, of the amount of funds awarded; and
a discussion of the efficacy of the program, including discussion of the metrics described in subsection (h).

subsection.text: The Secretary shall develop metrics for evaluating the performance of the program and the efficacy of the program in achieving the goals described in subsection (b).
In carrying out the activities under this section, the Secretary shall consult with stakeholders, including—

paragraph.text: other Federal agencies, including the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission;
the National Laboratories;
States;
tribal governments;
units of local government;
electric utilities, such as investor-owned electric utilities, publicly owned electric utilities, and electric cooperatives;
private companies, including energy technology manufacturers;
third-party energy service providers;
institutions of higher education; and
nonprofit organizations.

subsection.header: Personal protections for sensitive personal data

paragraph.text: In carrying out this section, the Secretary, the Administrator of the Energy Information Administration, and the Secretary of Homeland Security shall identify, incorporate, and follow best practices for protecting the privacy of individuals and businesses and the respective sensitive data of the individuals and businesses, including by managing privacy risk and implementing the Fair Information Practice Principles of the Federal Trade Commission for the collection, use, disclosure, and retention of individual electric consumer information in accordance with the Office of Management and Budget Circular A–130 (or successor circulars).

paragraph.header: Personal protections for sensitive personal data

subparagraph.text: No Federal entity shall request the creation, recording, or collection of data identified to an individual person as a result of the program.
All law enforcement agencies intending to request access to data regarding electricity consumption or generation shall be required—

clause.text: to produce a probable cause warrant as a requirement for gaining access to the data; and
to publicly report on the annual number of requests by that law enforcement agency for the data.

subsection.text: There are authorized to be appropriated to the Secretary to carry out this section—

paragraph.text: $225,000,000 for fiscal year 2020;
$275,000,000 for fiscal year 2021;
$325,000,000 for fiscal year 2022;
$400,000,000 for fiscal years 2023 through 2026;
$325,000,000 for fiscal year 2027;
$275,000,000 for fiscal year 2028; and
$225,000,000 for fiscal year 2029.
